source_text: Vt me satis contristat et animum nostrum grauiter affligit cum nulla mihi scribendi ad uos porrigitur occasio, detrimentum est enim meum uobiscum non colloqui, ita nihil mihi tantam laetitiam hilaritatemque restituit quam cum adest rursus occasio. uobiscum me esse arbitror, cum uobis per litteras loquor. quamquam igitur ita se haec habere quae dico certos uos esse sciam nec quicquam de uerborum meorum ueritate dubitare, tamen etiam argumentum sinceritatem rei asserit: namcam nulla prorsus praeteritur occasio, probatur affectio, quamuis ergo certus sim uos non minus esse in uitae actu graues quam in sacramento fideles: tamen, quoniam non desunt uitiorum assertores blandi et indulgentes patroni qui praestant uitiis auctoritatem et quod est deterius censuram scripturarum caelestium in aduocationem criminum conuertunt, quasi sine culpa innocens spectaculorum ad remissionem animi appetatur uoluptas – nam et eo usque eneruatus est ecclesiasticae disciplinae uigor et ita omni langore uitiorum praecipitatur peius ut non iam uitiis excusatio sed auctoritas detur — placuit paucis uos non nunc instruere, sed instructos admonere, ne quia male sunt uincta uulnera sanitatis obductae perrumpant cicatricem. nullum enim malum difficilius extinguitur quam quod faciles reditus habet, dum et multitudinis consensu asseritur et excusatione blanditur.
thought_title: Why Novatian writes: affection and warning
orientation: Novatian opens his treatise by explaining to his Christian readers why he is writing to them about public shows.
pass_a_gloss: As it saddens me enough and afflicts our mind heavily when no occasion of writing to you is offered to me, for it is my loss not to converse with you, so nothing restores to me such great joy and cheerfulness as when an occasion is present again. I think that I am with you, when I speak to you through letters. Although therefore I know that you are certain that these things which I say are so, and that you do not doubt at all about the truth of my words, yet also the argument asserts the sincerity of the matter: for since no occasion at all is passed over, affection is proved. Although therefore I may be sure that you are no less serious in the conduct of life than faithful in the sacrament: yet, since there are not lacking bland assertors of vices and indulgent patrons who furnish authority to vices and, what is worse, turn the censure of the heavenly scriptures into advocacy of crimes, as if without fault an innocent pleasure of public shows is sought for the relaxation of the mind — for even to that extent the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline has been weakened and so it is cast down headlong by all the languor of vices for the worse that no longer is an excuse given to vices but authority — it has pleased me to instruct you not now with a few words, but to admonish you already instructed, lest because wounds have been badly bound the scars of the healed skin break open. For no evil is extinguished with more difficulty than that which has easy returns, while it is both asserted by the consent of the multitude and flattered by excuse.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'public shows' for spectacula, not 'games' or 'spectacles'.
Glossary requires 'pleasure' for uoluptas, not 'delight' or 'enjoyment'.
Sacramentum here refers to the baptismal or Christian profession, rendered literally as 'sacrament' to preserve the technical sense.
Rendered as 'assertors' to keep the legal-advocacy flavor of the Latin, matching the brief's description of opponents as 'bland and indulgent patrons of vices'.
Literal rendering preserves the opponents' claim that shows are sought for mental relaxation.

pass_b_english: It saddens me deeply and weighs heavily on my heart whenever no opportunity to write to you presents itself, for it is my loss not to speak with you. So too, nothing restores such joy and cheer to me as when the opportunity comes again. I consider myself with you when I speak to you through letters. Although I know you are certain that what I say is true and do not doubt the truth of my words at all, still the very fact of my writing proves the sincerity of the matter: for no opportunity is ever passed over, and so my affection is demonstrated. Though I am sure you are no less serious in the conduct of your lives than you are faithful in the sacrament, still, since there is no lack of bland and indulgent patrons who lend authority to vices and, what is worse, turn the censure of the heavenly Scriptures into a defense of crimes—as if the pleasure of public shows were sought without fault or guilt for relaxation of the mind. For the vigor of church discipline has been so weakened and is so cast down headlong by every languor of vice, worse and worse, that vices are no longer given an excuse but an authority. So it has pleased a few not to instruct you now, but to admonish you who are already instructed, lest wounds that have been badly bound burst through the scar of healing. For no evil is more difficult to extinguish than one that has easy returns, while it is both asserted by the consensus of the crowd and flattered by excuse.

problems.why: Latin mentions only "bland and indulgent patrons"; the English adds "assertors of vices", a role not present in the source.
problems.ruling: Source says 'blandi et indulgentes patroni' (bland and indulgent patrons); English adds 'assertors of vices' not in Latin.

edits.old: bland assertors of vices and indulgent patrons

fixed: Removed 'assertors of vices' from the English: the source 'blandi et indulgentes patroni' mentions only 'bland and indulgent patrons', not assertors of vices.

problems.quote: So it has pleased me not to instruct you now, but to admonish you who are already instructed
problems.source_quote: placuit paucis vos non nunc instruere, sed instructos admonere
problems.why: Latin says 'it pleased a few', not 'me'; agency is changed.
problems.fix: Thus it has pleased a few that you not now be instructed, but that the instructed be admonished
problems.ruling: Latin 'placuit paucis' = 'it pleased a few'; English omits 'paucis' and says 'me', changing agency.

edits.old: So it has pleased me not to instruct you now, but to admonish you who are already instructed
edits.new: So it has pleased a few not to instruct you now, but to admonish you who are already instructed

fixed: Changed 'me' to 'a few' to match 'placuit paucis' (it pleased a few), preserving the source's agency.
